newsitem.title: USA: Oklahoma bomber Timothy McVeigh seeks new trial.
newsitem.headline: Oklahoma bomber Timothy McVeigh seeks new trial.

text.p: Attorneys for Timothy McVeigh, who was convicted last month of the Oklahoma City bombing and sentenced to death, asked for a new trial on Monday.

"Mr. McVeigh's life is literally at stake," lawyer Robert Nigh told reporters after the 180-page motion was filed with the trial court. He was accompanied by two other defence team members who wheeled into the courthouse more than a dozen boxes with 31 volumes of documents that constitute the motion.
Nigh said the motion also sought a lesser sentence.

McVeigh was convicted on June 2 of bombing the Alfred P. Murrah federal building in Oklahoma City on April 19, 1995, an attack that killed 168 people. On June 13 the same jury sentenced the Gulf War veteran to death.
"He (McVeigh) was anxious for this motion and brief to be filed," Nigh said. McVeigh has continued to be held in custody in suburban Denver since the end of his trial.

His lawyers cited overwhelming prejudicial pretrial publicity as one reason for seeking a new trial. "In the months and the weeks leading up to Mr. McVeigh's trial, there was a firestorm of adverse publicity that made it impossible for him to get a fair trial at that time," Nigh said.
The week before McVeigh's trial began on March 31 his lawyers had urged an appeals court to order it delayed on the same grounds.

Nigh cited victim impact testimony as another reason for granting a new trial. He called the testimony "simply overwhelming" and said "It triggered a decision that was not based upon reason but instead a decision that was based upon emotion," referring to often heart-wrenching testimony given by victims and relatives of people who died in the bombing.
Nigh said the request for a new trial was based on 15 grounds, many of them technical legal reasons. Defence lawyers routinely file requests for new trials and are usually denied.
But Nigh, without explaining, said Monday's filing was not routine. He declined to predict when he expected U.S. District Court Judge Richard Matsh to make a decision on the motion.
The defence attorneys are also basing their argument for a new trial on the judge's refusal to allow into evidence a report that was highly critical of procedures in the FBI's crime laboratory.
They also cited the judge's refusal to allow testimony from a government informant who would have said that white extremists in eastern Oklahoma had discussed blowing up federal buildings.
If the motion for a new trial is denied by Matsch, the defence attorneys have said they will appeal the conviction.
McVeigh's alleged co-conspirator, Terry Nichols, is scheduled to go on trial on Sept. 29 in Denver. Prosecutors are also seeking the death penalty for Nichols.
